devices.title: CC1101 radio module
devices.summary: A radio link to Somfy RTS awnings.
devices.body:
# CC1101 radio module: wiring and setup

A CC1101 433 MHz transceiver, the Ebyte **E07-M1101D** with an SMA antenna socket, on an M5Stack
Atom Lite that runs ESPSomfy-RTS: the `awnings` component's node, which sends and hears Somfy RTS.
Device file: [cc1101.yaml](https://github.com/zerostorypoints/domosenso/blob/5b012718dcce57a386b1f3cfe87b8d7512c39b2f/devices/cc1101.yaml).

## Wiring

![E07-M1101D on an M5Stack Atom Lite: eight wires from G, 3V3, G22, G21, G33, G23, G19, G25 to module pins 1 to 8, and a 433 MHz antenna on the SMA socket](/wiring/cc1101-atom-lite.svg)

| E07-M1101D pin | signal | Atom Lite (bottom header) | wire | ESPSomfy-RTS, Radio page |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | GND | G | black | |
| 2 | VCC | 3V3 (**never 5V**) | red | |
| 3 | GDO0 | G22 | purple | TX 22 |
| 4 | CSN | G21 | orange | CSN 21 |
| 5 | SCK | G33 | yellow | SCLK 33 |
| 6 | MOSI | G23 | blue | MOSI 23 |
| 7 | MISO | G19 | green | MISO 19 |
| 8 | GDO2 | G25 | white | RX 25 |

Pin 1 has the square pad. The pinout is the one the ESPSomfy-RTS wiki gives for this module; it is
the wiring of the first home's node. The Atom's 5V and the Grove port stay free. Another CC1101
board (a different maker) can number its pins differently: go by the signal names printed on it,
not by the numbers.

## The antenna

- Screw a **433 MHz** antenna onto the SMA socket before the node transmits. A CC1101 sending into
  an open socket can damage its output stage (general radio practice, not seen here).
- The antenna decides what the node hears. One home's wind sensor reached the node at −83 to
  −86 dBm and only part of its reports arrived, with gaps of hours (`components/awnings/README.md`).
  Stand the antenna upright and move the node, or the antenna on a short cable, towards the
  sensor and the awnings; keep it clear of metal.

## Firmware and first start

ESPSomfy-RTS is a release binary flashed over USB with `esptool`, then set up in its own web
page: the network, then on the Radio page the pins of the right-hand column above, then MQTT and a
virtual remote per awning. The commands and steps: `components/awnings/README.md`, "Flashing the
node". The radio answers when `GET http://<node>/controller` shows
`transceiver.config.radioInit: true`; `false` means the CC1101 did not answer on SPI with these pins
(a wire on the wrong socket, or VCC missing).

## When it does not work

| what you see | likely cause |
|---|---|
| `radioInit: false` | a wire on the wrong socket, the pins in ESPSomfy's Radio page not matching the wiring, or VCC not on 3V3 |
| awnings do not move, the node logs sending | no antenna, or the virtual remote not paired with the awning |
| the node hears the handsets only sometimes | reception: antenna position and distance |

The second and third rows are inference from how RTS works, apart from reception, which the first
home saw.

devices.title: HLK-LD2410C radar
devices.body:
# HLK-LD2410C radar: wiring and setup

A Hi-Link HLK-LD2410C 24 GHz presence radar on an M5Stack Atom Lite that already runs as a
`bermuda-presence` BLE proxy. It is that component's optional feature `radar`; the Ramka uses a
radar like this to wake its screen. Device file: [hlk-ld2410c.yaml](https://github.com/zerostorypoints/domosenso/blob/5b012718dcce57a386b1f3cfe87b8d7512c39b2f/devices/hlk-ld2410c.yaml).

## Wiring

![HLK-LD2410C on an M5Stack Atom Lite: 5V to VCC, G to GND, G22 to TX, G19 to RX, OUT not connected](/wiring/hlk-ld2410c-atom-lite.svg)

| Atom Lite (bottom header) | HLK-LD2410C | wire | why |
|---|---|---|---|
| 5V | VCC | red | the module needs 5 V; **never 3V3** |
| G | GND | black | |
| G22 | TX | purple | the Atom receives on G22 (`rx_pin: GPIO22`) |
| G19 | RX | green | the Atom sends on G19 (`tx_pin: GPIO19`) |
| — | OUT | — | not connected: presence comes over the UART |

Source: `components/bermuda-presence/esphome/ld2410.yaml`, the wiring of the first home's boards.
The labels are the ones printed on the Atom and on the module; the diagram shows which socket goes to
which pin, not where they sit on the boards. Colours are a convention: any colour works if both ends
match. The Grove port stays free.

## Firmware

The board's thin device file pulls the radar package next to the proxy package; with
`radar: true` on that proxy in the component's inputs, `domosenso add` writes it so (SPEC-015):

```yaml
packages:
  proxy: github://zerostorypoints/domosenso/components/bermuda-presence/esphome/ble-proxy.yaml@bermuda-presence/<version>
  radar: github://zerostorypoints/domosenso/components/bermuda-presence/esphome/ld2410.yaml@bermuda-presence/<version>
```

Then `esphome config`, `compile` and a flash, as for any proxy (`components/bermuda-presence/README.md`).
The UART runs at 256000 baud, the module's factory setting.

## After the first start

- The module keeps its settings (gates, thresholds, timeout, its own Bluetooth) in its own flash:
  set them once from Home Assistant; they survive a reflash of the Atom.
- Engineering mode is the one setting it forgets on a restart, and the light reading only comes in
  engineering frames, so the package switches it back on 10 s after every boot.
- New entities on the proxy's device: presence, moving and still target, detection distance and
  the others listed under `features.radar` in `components/bermuda-presence/component.yaml`.

## When it does not work

| what you see | likely cause |
|---|---|
| no radar entities at all | the device file lacks the `radar:` package line |
| radar entities `unavailable` or never changing | TX and RX swapped (TX must go to G22), or VCC on 3V3 |
| the Atom resets or drops off Wi-Fi when the radar is plugged in | a weak USB supply: the radar draws its power through the Atom; use a plain 5 V USB supply (the `power` note on `ble-proxy` in `components/bermuda-presence/component.yaml`) |
| presence that never clears with nobody there | sensitivity and gates, set from Home Assistant; the module keeps them |

The last two rows are inference from how the module and the board are powered and set up, not
cases seen in the first home.

devices.title: TCL wall tablet
devices.summary: Companion app, screen behavior and the tested landscape layout.
devices.body:
# Setting up the Ramka's tablet

From a reset Android tablet to the Ramka on screen, with the TCL NXTPAPER 11 Plus (9469X,
Android 16, `devices/tcl-9469x.yaml`) as the worked example. Other makers name the menus
differently; what each setting is for is said next to it, so the same switch can be found
elsewhere. The reasons behind the settings and the Companion app's quirks:
[the ramka field notes](https://github.com/zerostorypoints/domosenso/blob/5b012718dcce57a386b1f3cfe87b8d7512c39b2f/components/ramka/README.md#the-tablet).

The paths for the screen lock, the WebView version, app pinning and the Companion app's own
settings were written down on the tested TCL. The others (system update, special app access,
developer options) are stock Android 16 paths, not checked on it. The `adb` line next to a setting
does the same from a computer, with USB debugging on (Settings → About tablet → tap *Build
number* seven times, then Settings → System → Developer options → *USB debugging*).

## 1. In Home Assistant, before the tablet

- **A user for the tablet.** Settings → People → Add person, *Allow login* on, *Administrator*
  off, *Can only log in from the local network* on if the tablet never leaves home. The tablet
  signs in as this user, never as you: the device and its entities get registered under it, and
  kiosk-mode hides the header and sidebar for this user only. Its user name goes into the
  `kiosk_user` input.
- **kiosk-mode** (optional): HACS → Frontend → *kiosk-mode* (NemesisRE). Without it the Ramka
  shows Home Assistant's header and sidebar. `?disable_km` on a URL shows them again.

## 2. Android

| what | where on the TCL | why | `adb` instead |
|---|---|---|---|
| Android updates | Settings → System → System update | the WebView below needs a current Android | — |
| *Android System WebView* 123 or newer | Play Store → update; the version: Settings → Apps → See all apps → Android System WebView, at the bottom | the cards import JSON modules; older WebViews do not load them | `adb shell dumpsys package com.google.android.webview \| grep versionName` |
| **Screen lock: None** | Settings → Security → Screen lock → None | the package wakes the screen; with a PIN or a swipe it stops on the lock screen | `adb shell locksettings set-disabled true` (only while no PIN is set) |
| NXTPAPER key: **Color Paper** | the NXTPAPER key at the right end of the top edge | Ink Paper turns photos and album art grey; Home Assistant cannot switch the mode | — |
| charge limit | none on this model; it stops at 80 % on the charger by itself | protects the battery on a tablet that never leaves the charger; on a tablet without a limit, use its battery-protection setting or a smart plug | — |

## 3. The Companion app

Install *Home Assistant* (`io.homeassistant.companion.android`) from the Play Store. 2026.8.4 or
newer if the Play Store offers it: 2026.6.5 can keep the screen on for good (field notes).

**Permissions**, Settings → Apps → Home Assistant (the app asks for the first two while it is set up;
if they were refused, they are under *Advanced* or Settings → Apps → Special app access):

| permission | value | without it | `adb` instead |
|---|---|---|---|
| *Modify system settings* | allowed | brightness and screen-timeout commands are dropped without a word | `adb shell appops set io.homeassistant.companion.android WRITE_SETTINGS allow` |
| *Display over other apps* | allowed | the app cannot come to the front after a wake; `app_importance` reads `cached` | `adb shell appops set io.homeassistant.companion.android SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW allow` |
| Battery → *Unrestricted* (battery optimisation **off**) | unrestricted | Android stops the app in the background and the commands stop arriving | `adb shell dumpsys deviceidle whitelist +io.homeassistant.companion.android` |
| Notifications | allowed | — | — |
| Location | may be denied | — | — |

**Sign in** to your Home Assistant's local URL as the tablet's user (section 1).

**App settings**, in the app: Settings → Companion app:

| setting | value | why |
|---|---|---|
| Device name | short, lower case, e.g. `ramka` | becomes `notify.mobile_app_<slug>` and `sensor.<slug>_*`, which go into the `tablet_device` input; set it before the first sign-in finishes, or rename the entities afterwards |
| **Keep screen on** | **off** | with it on the screen never sleeps; the package keeps the screen awake through Android's screen timeout instead |
| Fullscreen | on | hides Android's status and navigation bars |
| Screen orientation | Landscape | the tested layout is landscape |
| Always show first view on app start | on | after Android kills the app it comes back on the Ramka, not on the last page |
| Persistent connection | Always | commands arrive over the local websocket, not Firebase: no internet dependency, no delay |
| Manage sensors | on: `light_sensor`, `battery_level`, `app_importance`, `charger_type`, `battery_temperature`, `is_charging`; for your own view also `interactive`, `battery_state`, `battery_health` | the package reads the first six; a disabled sensor is missing from Home Assistant |
| Sensor update frequency | Fast always | once a minute; the slower settings drop to 15 minutes and brightness lags behind the room |

**Profile**, in the app as the tablet's user (the person icon at the bottom of the sidebar):
*Dashboard* = the Ramka's (`dashboard_path`, `dashboard-ramka` by default), *Language* and *Time
format* as the dashboard's language, *Theme* dark. Once kiosk-mode is active the profile page is
hidden: set these first, or open the profile with `?disable_km`.

**App pinning: leave it off.** Pinning (Settings → Security → App pinning) keeps a guest inside
the app, but it also blocks the way to unstick a screen that will not sleep (`command_launch_app`
to Android's Settings and back, field notes). The Ramka's two top corners are its way out
instead: top-left opens `exit_left`, top-right reloads the Ramka with kiosk-mode off.

## 4. Measure, render, check

1. `domosenso probe <target> --install`, open `<HA URL>/domosenso-probe/0` in the Companion app
   with the tablet in its final orientation, `domosenso probe <target> --read`, then
   `domosenso probe <target> --remove`. The `viewport` goes into the `screen` input; `webview`
   under 123 or `json-modules no` means the cards will not load; `user admin` means the app is
   signed in as an administrator (section 1).
2. Fill the inputs (`tablet_device`, `screen`, `kiosk_user`, the radar), render, deploy to staging,
   look at the shots, then production. Press `input_button.<prefix>_reload` once the tablet shows
   the dashboard.
3. With nobody near the radar for `off_delay_s` the screen goes dark; walking in wakes it on the
   ambient page. `sensor.<slug>_app_importance` reads `foreground` while the screen is on and
   `top_sleeping` while it sleeps.

| symptom | look at |
|---|---|
| the screen never sleeps | *Keep screen on* (section 3); on Companion 2026.6.5 see the field notes |
| it wakes onto the lock screen | Screen lock (section 2) |
| brightness never changes, the screen never times out | *Modify system settings* |
| it wakes on the launcher or another app, `app_importance` = `cached` | *Display over other apps* |
| commands arrive late or not at all after a while | battery *Unrestricted*, *Persistent connection* |
| a sensor the package needs is `unavailable` or missing | Manage sensors |
| the cards stay empty or show "Custom element doesn't exist" | the WebView version |
| English words on a Polish (or German) dashboard | the profile's language |

articles.title: Try it before it reaches your home
articles.summary: Every change can now be opened in a local Home Assistant first, by anyone, without writing code.
articles.author: DomoSenso
articles.body:
DomoSenso now has a shared way of working that is open to anyone. Contributors use a fork and run the same checks as the core team. An AI agent reviews each change, and a human approves it. Nobody can approve their own pull request, and that includes the maintainers.

## Look at a pull request before it is accepted

Ask Codex or Claude Code to run `preview-pr` for a pull request number. It starts a fictional home on your computer with the real Ramka on screen. You can switch it between morning, evening, away and rain. It has no lights, speakers or blinds of its own; light switches and music commands are only recorded. When you have seen enough, you accept the change or ask for changes.

## Test an update on your own home

`stage-home-update` does the same for your own home. It sets up a separate Home Assistant with no access to your network or the internet, and with none of your passwords. It loads the configuration you have now, then the update, and compares the two. In the first run on a real home, three component updates went through and every entity, automation and dashboard came out the same. The only difference was the new address of the Ramka's cards.

## Still to come

A test Home Assistant starts empty, so the tiles on the dashboards have no readings. Next it will be able to show real readings copied from your own Home Assistant, or realistic invented ones when none are available.

articles.title: From a component to the wires
articles.summary: Two documented Atom connections, plus the tablet setup they help support.
articles.author: DomoSenso
articles.body:
Hardware requirements should lead to instructions you can inspect.

The [HLK-LD2410C radar guide](/devices/hlk-ld2410c/) pairs a labeled wiring diagram with a pin table, firmware steps and first-start checks. The [CC1101 guide](/devices/cc1101/) does the same for the radio node used with Somfy RTS awnings.

## Same board, different jobs

The radar accompanies an ESPHome Bluetooth proxy. The CC1101 radio node runs ESPSomfy-RTS. These are distinct firmware roles; one board should not be presented as doing both jobs at once.

## Finish at the screen

The [tablet setup guide](/devices/tcl-9469x/) covers the Companion app and Android settings used by the documented Ramka installation. Wiring, firmware, integration and presentation are separate steps, and each needs a check.

These guides describe the documented models and connections. They do not establish support for all related boards, radios or meters.

articles.title: Keep only the pages you need
articles.summary: The status page can now be removed from Ramka’s ambient rotation.
articles.author: DomoSenso
articles.body:
Ramka 0.3.0 adds `status_page: false`. It removes the read-only status page from both the rotation and the swipe sequence. Status remains enabled by default.

## When to use it

If the controls already show your lights and awnings, and there are no other status items you want to see, the extra ambient page may add little. You can keep the useful pages and leave that one out.

Climate, air, plants and photos still depend on their own inputs. At least one ambient page must remain; a render with no ambient pages fails rather than leaving an empty rotation.

## Upgrade deliberately

Review the release notes linked below. Update the component in your separate home project, adjust the inputs, render and inspect the resulting pages. Review the deployment plan before changing a live installation.

The release was merged on 27 October 2026. This article’s publication date is 28 October; it is not the tag creation date.

articles.title: A tablet, a radar, an ordinary shelf
articles.summary: Inside the maintainer’s first installation: components with a physical home.
articles.author: DomoSenso
articles.body:
The first installation brings an Android tablet, a nearby radar and Home Assistant together. This is the maintainer’s personal setup, not a customer project. The photographs were already published in the original installation journal.

## Give the screen a reason to wake

Ramka supplies the ambient pages and controls. The radar supplies presence and distance through the optional radar feature of Room presence. Bluetooth room estimates and radar presence are separate signals; the screen does not need to identify a person to react to someone nearby.

## Show what is already happening

The media integration supplies a Home Assistant media player. Ramka can use its track metadata for the now-playing view. The documented player is a Hegel H400; a speaker visible in a photograph is not a claim about compatibility.

## What this installation taught us

A wall display needs more than a dashboard layout. Screen wake and sleep, Android permissions, charging behavior and the viewport all matter. The [tablet guide](/devices/tcl-9469x/) records the tested setup; the [radar guide](/devices/hlk-ld2410c/) records the wiring.

The original journal documented Ramka 0.2.0. This article does not establish which version is running in the home today. Field experience remains limited; another installation needs its own validation.

articles.title: A dashboard should fit the home it lives in
articles.summary: Ramka 0.2.0 made climate, air, plants and photos conditional on your inputs.
articles.author: DomoSenso
articles.body:
Not every home has plant sensors. Not every tablet needs a photo album.

In Ramka 0.2.0, climate, air, plants and photos became optional. Leave out an input and the corresponding page is left out of the rendered dashboard and its rotation. The shared component stays the same; each home decides what belongs on its screen.

## Before upgrading

Read the pinned release notes below, review your inputs and render the dashboard before applying changes. This historical article retains the date and subject of the original homepage entry. The [current component page](/components/ramka/) may describe a newer release.

howTos.title: Automate old awnings
howTos.description: Awnings with a Somfy remote can retract at sunset and follow the wind sensor without rewiring. Wall-button motors are coming soon.

branches.situation: A motor with a Somfy RTS remote
branches.needs: A small radio node: an M5Stack Atom Lite with a CC1101 radio module running ESPSomfy-RTS. It pairs with each awning as one more remote.
branches.wiring: None at the awning. Eight short wires between the radio module and the Atom, on the desk.
branches.prompt: Add the awnings component to my home, prepare the radio node for my Somfy RTS awnings (I will flash it myself), and stop before production so I can check it on staging.

branches.situation: A motor with buttons in the wall
branches.needs: A Shelly 2PM behind the wall switch; the buttons keep working.

branches.situation: A Somfy io motor (a two-way remote)
branches.needs: Somfy io is a different radio from RTS; the RTS node cannot drive it.

branches.situation: No motor (a crank or a strap)
branches.needs: An awning cannot be automated without a motor. Fitting one is a job for an awning installer.

howTos.body:
If your awnings already open and close with a Somfy remote, you can automate them without
touching the awnings or the wiring: a small radio node learns to speak to them as one more remote,
and Home Assistant then retracts them at sunset and shows them on your phone and wall tablet. Your
old remote keeps working.

Look at your remote first: the label on the back or in the battery compartment usually says RTS
or io. RTS is the older one-way radio this guide covers; Somfy io is a different radio, not
supported yet. Awnings run by buttons in the wall need a relay behind the switch; that branch
waits for the Shelly component ([issue #74](https://github.com/zerostorypoints/domosenso/issues/74)).

## A motor with a Somfy RTS remote

**What to buy**

- One [M5Stack Atom Lite](/devices/m5stack-atom-lite/), about €8–15.
- One [CC1101 radio module](/devices/cc1101/) (tested: Ebyte E07-M1101D) with a 433 MHz antenna,
  about €5–10.
- A USB power supply for the node.

**Wiring.** Nothing at the awning. The radio module connects to the Atom with eight short wires;
the [CC1101 guide](/devices/cc1101/) has the diagram and the pin table. The module runs on 3.3 V,
never 5 V, and the antenna goes on before the node transmits.

**What your agent does, and what you do.** The agent adds the [awnings component](/components/awnings/)
to your home, prepares the flashing commands and the node's settings, and puts the awnings on your
staging Home Assistant. You flash the node over USB, join its Wi-Fi from your phone once, and pair
the awnings. Nothing reaches your real Home Assistant until you say so.

**What you get**

- Each awning as a cover in Home Assistant, with open, stop and close on your phone and on the
  [Ramka](/components/ramka/) wall tablet.
- At sunset, every awning that is not closed retracts by itself.
- The wind sensor's reports are watched, and you get an alert if it goes silent. The awnings still
  retract on wind by themselves, as before.
- Home Assistant follows the old remote too: when someone uses it, the positions update.

**Hints from real installations**

- Pair one awning at a time: hold PROG on a remote that already works for that awning, then pair
  the node's virtual remote. Name each awning as you go, before you pair the next one.
- Somfy RTS only sends, it never answers. Home Assistant knows what it sent, not where the awning
  is, and estimates the position from travel time. Time each awning's full extend and retract once
  and enter it on the node; the default of 10 seconds is wrong for most awnings.
- The node may hear the wind sensor only part of the time. On one installation the sensor was
  heard only intermittently, and the "sensor silent" alert had to be relaxed to 72 hours to stop
  false alarms. Place the node, or its antenna, with a clear line to the awnings and the sensor.
- The node prints your Wi-Fi password in its start-up log. Never paste that log into a chat or an
  issue.
- Reserve the node's address in your router so it comes back after a power cut.

howTos.title: Know your air quality
howTos.description: Know when to open a window. One air monitor shows CO₂, fine dust and an air-quality score on your phone and a wall tablet.

branches.needs: A Ruuvi Air and one Bluetooth proxy within range (an M5Stack Atom Lite), unless you already have one.
branches.wiring: None. The monitor and the proxy each plug into USB power.
branches.prompt: Add the air part of the climate-air component to my home with my Ruuvi Air, show it on my wall tablet, and stop before production so I can check it on staging.

branches.situation: A CO₂ or air-quality sensor already in Home Assistant, another brand
branches.needs: Nothing new. The component reads the CO₂, fine-dust and index sensors Home Assistant already shows; only the Ruuvi Air has been tested.
branches.prompt: Add the air part of the climate-air component to my home using the air-quality sensor I already have in Home Assistant, and stop before production so I can check it on staging.

howTos.body:
Stale air is easy to miss and easy to measure: a CO₂ reading tells you when to open a window, and
above about 1000 ppm most people notice it as tiredness or a stuffy room. One air monitor in the
room you spend most time in, read by Home Assistant, puts that number on your phone and on a wall
tablet, next to fine dust and an overall air-quality score.

If you only want temperature and humidity per room, see
[Room temperature you can see](/how-to/see-room-temperature/); this guide is about the air itself.

## No air monitor yet

**What to buy**

- A [Ruuvi Air](/devices/ruuvi-air/), a Bluetooth monitor for CO₂, fine dust (PM2.5), VOC, NOx,
  temperature, humidity and pressure.
- One Bluetooth proxy within range, an [M5Stack Atom Lite](/devices/m5stack-atom-lite/), about
  €8–15, unless you already have one, for example from
  [room presence](/how-to/presence-who-is-home/). The monitor needs no proxy of its own.

**Wiring.** None. Both run on USB power.

**What your agent does, and what you do.** Home Assistant discovers the monitor through the
proxy; you confirm it, switch on its air-quality score (off by default) and switch off the
light-level reading the monitor does not have. The agent adds the air part of the
[climate-air component](/components/climate-air/) and shows the result on your staging Home
Assistant first.

**What you get**

- CO₂, PM2.5, VOC and NOx and an air-quality score out of 100, the same score the Ruuvi app shows.
- An air page on the [Ramka](/components/ramka/) wall tablet.
- History of every figure, so you can see which hours of the day the air gets bad.

## A sensor already in Home Assistant

The component takes the CO₂, PM2.5, VOC, NOx and score sensors as inputs, whichever of them your
sensor has. Only the Ruuvi Air has been tested; check the readings on staging before you rely on
them.

## Hints from real installations

- Place the monitor at breathing height, where people sit, not next to the hob or an open window.
- Through the common Atom Lite proxies the Ruuvi Air reported CO₂, temperature, humidity and PM2.5,
  but not PM1, PM4 or PM10: those travel in a newer Bluetooth format the proxies do not receive.
- VOC and NOx need about a day after power-on to settle. Do not judge them, or set alerts on them,
  before that.
- The monitor has a fan. Next to a presence radar it can look like movement; check the radar after
  placing it.

howTos.title: Music in every room
howTos.description: Control the music you already play from a wall tablet and your phone, starting from the network player or speakers you have.

branches.situation: A network streamer or amplifier Home Assistant supports
branches.needs: Nothing new. The player's Home Assistant integration (tested with a Hegel H400 through hegel_streaming).
branches.wiring: None. The player is on your home network.
branches.prompt: Add the media component to my home for the network player I already have, show it on my wall tablet, and stop before production so I can check it on staging.

branches.situation: Speakers in several rooms that you group in their own app
branches.needs: DomoSenso controls one player from the wall tablet; grouping rooms stays in the speakers' own app.

branches.situation: An old hi-fi or passive speakers, nothing on the network
branches.needs: A network streamer in front of the amplifier first; Home Assistant has nothing to talk to without one.
branches.wiring: The streamer's audio cable to the amplifier.

howTos.body:
You do not need new speakers to control music from the wall: if your streamer, amplifier or
speaker already shows up in Home Assistant, DomoSenso puts it on a wall tablet and your phone with
play, pause, volume, input and what is playing now. This guide starts from the player you have.

Two things it does not do today. It does not group rooms: one player is shown, and speakers that
play together are grouped in their own app. And it does not make an old hi-fi smart; that needs a
network streamer in front of it first.

## A network streamer or amplifier Home Assistant supports

**What to buy.** Nothing, if Home Assistant already lists your player as a media player. The tested
player is a [Hegel H400](/devices/hegel-h400/) through the `hegel_streaming` integration, which
finds the amplifier on your network without an account. Other players work when they offer the
basics the wall tablet needs: on and off, play and pause, volume and the current track. Only the
Hegel has been tested.

**Wiring.** None. The player stays where it is.

**What your agent does, and what you do.** The agent adds the [media component](/components/media/)
and points the [Ramka](/components/ramka/) wall tablet at your player, on your staging Home
Assistant first. You install the player's integration if Home Assistant does not have it yet
(the Hegel one comes from HACS) and confirm when the player is discovered.

**What you get**

- A now-playing page on the wall tablet with the title, artist and cover art when the player
  reports them, and the audio quality on the Hegel.
- Play, pause, volume and turn on from the tablet or your phone.
- Previous and next hidden while a service that cannot skip is playing, so the buttons on screen
  are the ones that work.

**Hints from real installations**

- Home Assistant may list the same amplifier two or three times (for example through Cast and
  DLNA as well). Point the tablet at the player from its own integration.
- Resume and skip depend on the player's integration and the streaming service. Before you rely
  on it, pause from the wall tablet and press play again: the same track should continue. On one
  installation Spotify Connect lost the session on a plain play until the integration was fixed.
- A player switched off at the mains does not answer at all. Network standby keeps it reachable.

howTos.title: Presence: who is home, and in which room
howTos.description: See who is home and which room they are in, from the phones and watches people already carry, with small Bluetooth receivers.

branches.needs: One Bluetooth proxy per room, an M5Stack Atom Lite, and the Bermuda integration in Home Assistant.
branches.wiring: None. Each proxy plugs into a USB power supply.
branches.prompt: Add the bermuda-presence component to my home with one Bluetooth proxy per room, prepare the proxies' firmware (I will flash them myself), and stop before production so I can check it on staging.

branches.situation: Someone in the room without a phone
branches.needs: An HLK-LD2410C radar on one of the room's proxies. It notices a person sitting still and wakes the wall tablet.
branches.wiring: Four low-voltage wires between the radar and the Atom.
branches.prompt: Add the radar feature of the bermuda-presence component to the proxy next to my wall tablet, let it wake the Ramka, and stop before production so I can check it on staging.

branches.needs: These trackers change their Bluetooth address and cannot be told apart as one person's tag.

howTos.body:
Home Assistant can tell who is home and which room they are in from the phones and watches people
already carry: a small Bluetooth receiver in each room hears them, and the Bermuda integration
works out which room is closest. DomoSenso turns that into one line per room ("Alex, Sam"), shown on
your phone and on a wall tablet. A radar next to the tablet adds "someone is here" for people
without a phone in their pocket.

## Phones and watches everyone carries

**What to buy**

- One [M5Stack Atom Lite](/devices/m5stack-atom-lite/) per room, about €8–15 each. A room without
  one gets no presence of its own.
- A plain 5 V USB power supply for each. Fast-charging plugs can cut the Atom's power.

**Wiring.** None. Each proxy sits on a shelf or in a socket, wherever it is out of the way.

**What your agent does, and what you do.** The agent adds the
[bermuda-presence component](/components/bermuda-presence/), writes one firmware file per proxy
and the room sensors, and shows them on your staging Home Assistant first. You flash the proxies
over USB, install Bermuda (it comes from HACS) and add each phone and watch. Apple devices change
their Bluetooth address, so each one needs its identity key once; the
[component's notes](/components/bermuda-presence/) explain how to read it.

**What you get**

- One sensor per room with the names of the people in it, and a tablet left in a room shown in
  brackets, because a tablet lies where it was put down.
- A notification when a proxy has been offline for ten minutes.
- Room sensors your own automations can use.

## Someone in the room without a phone

**What to buy.** One [HLK-LD2410C radar](/devices/hlk-ld2410c/), about €3–10, on the Atom that is
already the room's proxy.

**Wiring.** Four wires between the radar and the Atom, all low voltage: 5 V, ground and two data
lines. The [radar guide](/devices/hlk-ld2410c/) has the diagram.

**What you get.** A "someone is in the room" sensor that works without a phone, and the
[Ramka](/components/ramka/) wall tablet waking when someone comes near.

## Hints from real installations

- Cover every room before you calibrate. A room without a proxy is never empty: Bermuda places
  the person in the nearest room that has one.
- One flat needed seven proxies, one per room.
- Phones and watches work best. Tested with iPhones, iPads and Apple Watches; Garmin watches stay
  silent while connected to their phone.
- Give each proxy a fixed address in your router so it comes back after a power cut.
- Keep Bermuda's distance sensors out of Home Assistant's history. On one installation they filled
  most of the database.
- The radar does not see a person sitting still within about 1.5 m of it, only movement. Mount it
  a little away from where people sit closest.

howTos.title: See your power consumption
howTos.description: Find the devices that never really switch off with a small metering relay behind a socket. Coming with the Shelly component.

branches.situation: A device you suspect of drawing power in standby
branches.needs: A small metering relay (a Shelly PM Mini) behind its socket.

howTos.body:
A small metering relay behind one socket shows how much the device plugged into it draws, on your
phone and in Home Assistant's energy history, including the standby draw of devices that never
really switch off. DomoSenso does not cover this yet: it waits for the Shelly component
([issue #74](https://github.com/zerostorypoints/domosenso/issues/74)), and this guide is published
when that component is released.

## Hints from real installations

- On one installation a metering relay behind an amplifier's socket showed its standby draw, the
  kind of figure that is hard to see any other way.
- Fitting a relay behind a socket is mains work. Have an electrician do it.

howTos.title: Room temperature you can see
howTos.description: See the temperature and humidity of every room at a glance, on your phone and a wall tablet, from small battery sensors.

branches.needs: One Tapo T315 thermo-hygrometer per room and a Tapo hub (tested with the H200) that they report to.
branches.wiring: None. Battery sensors; the hub plugs into a socket and joins your network.
branches.prompt: Add the climate-air component to my home with one Tapo sensor per room, show the rooms on my wall tablet, and stop before production so I can check it on staging.

branches.situation: Temperature sensors already in Home Assistant, another brand
branches.needs: Nothing new. The component reads any temperature and humidity sensors Home Assistant already shows; only Tapo has been tested.
branches.prompt: Add the climate-air component to my home using the temperature and humidity sensors I already have in Home Assistant, one entry per room, and stop before production so I can check it on staging.

howTos.body:
To see every room's temperature in one place, put one small battery sensor in each room and let
Home Assistant collect them: DomoSenso turns them into a room list, a whole-home average and the
most humid room, on your phone and on a wall tablet. If you already have sensors in Home Assistant,
you can use those instead.

## No room sensors yet

**What to buy**

- One Tapo T315 temperature and humidity sensor per room, about €20–30 each. It has its own small
  display, so the reading is also on the wall.
- One Tapo hub that the sensors report to (tested: the H200).

**Wiring.** None. The sensors run on batteries; the hub plugs into a socket and joins your
network.

**What your agent does, and what you do.** You set up the hub and the sensors in the Tapo app and
add your TP-Link account in Home Assistant once; after that the hub is read on your home network.
The agent adds the [climate-air component](/components/climate-air/) with one entry per room,
labels them the way your household names the rooms, and shows the result on your staging Home
Assistant first.

**What you get**

- Temperature and humidity for every room, the indoor average, warmest and coolest, and, from
  your weather service or an outdoor sensor, the difference to outside.
- The most humid room by name, and a flag when the bathroom stays humid for ten minutes.
- The sensor with the lowest battery, before one goes flat.
- History kept as hourly figures, so you can compare this winter with the last.
- A temperature page on the [Ramka](/components/ramka/) wall tablet.

## Temperature sensors already in Home Assistant

The component takes each room's temperature and humidity sensor as an input, whatever their
brand. Your agent lists the ones Home Assistant has and asks which room each belongs to. Only the
Tapo sensors have been tested; tell your agent which ones you have, and check the readings on
staging before you rely on them.

## Hints from real installations

- Put each sensor away from radiators, windows and direct sun, at roughly head height. A sensor on
  a sunny windowsill reports the sun, not the room.
- Leave a glazed porch or winter garden out of the indoor average if its windows are often open;
  it still shows as a room of its own.
- Tapo hides the battery and signal entities by default. Switch on the battery ones in Home
  Assistant, or the lowest-battery figure stays empty.
- Reserve the hub's address in your router so Home Assistant finds it after a power cut.
